cards.heading: Three tiers by residence
cards.question: What are the three tiers of agent instruction layering, split by when they should occupy context?
cards.answer: An always-on project config file (few rules for every task), on-demand procedure files that load only when their declared trigger matches, and the live prompt carrying what's unique to the current task.

cards.heading: Instructions must earn residence
cards.question: Why does agent instruction layering treat every resident token as needing to 'earn its residence'?
cards.answer: Every resident token competes with every other token for the model's finite attention, so an instruction has to earn residence rather than merely be true.

cards.heading: Default behavior with no project file
cards.question: What does a model default to when there's no always-on project configuration file?
cards.answer: Whatever was most plausible in its training data (e.g. the wrong package manager, wrong formatter, defensive boilerplate) — not the project's actual conventions.

cards.heading: On-demand files route on metadata
cards.question: How do on-demand procedure files keep their cost near zero until they're relevant?
cards.answer: They route on metadata — a name and description, optionally narrowed by file-path patterns — so the routing decision costs a line, and the full body enters context only when it matches.

cards.heading: Benchmark: curated beats self-generated
cards.question: What did the eighty-six-task skills benchmark show about curated versus self-generated procedures?
cards.answer: Human-curated written procedures let a small cheap model outscore the flagship model working without them; letting a model generate its own procedures erased the gain entirely.
